---
title: "How I teach"
description: "Why I love teaching, what I think good science needs from a group, and how I run my time with students."
toc: true
---

My first student was my brother. He was three, I was ten, and I had decided
that he needed to understand how maths works. It went better than you would
expect. He later skipped a year and sailed through school, so either the
method worked or I made him stupidly smart, and I am not sure which. I
learned something too: explaining a thing to someone who does not yet know
it is the most fun you can have with an idea. I have not changed my mind
since.

In the years after that I taught maths tutorials, first for physicists and
later for biochemists, gave guest lectures in machine learning and in
*Theoretical Neuroscience*, ran the computational neuroscience seminar with
its sessions on how to read a paper, how to write one, and how to design a
figure, and supervised Bachelor's and Master's theses. The
[interactive pages](index.qmd) on this site come from the same impulse.^[An
impulse is, physically speaking, what it takes to overcome inertia. Inertia
is also what my family name means, more or less, so I have had to deal with
the pun for a while.] This page is about what I have come to believe along
the way. Believe is a strong word. I use it because it best captures the
state of my knowledge: firmly held, and incomplete.

## Learning happens with your hands

I am convinced that you learn something when you do it, not when you hear
about it. For science that means, to me, doing the mathematics, even though
I never formally studied it. You have to force yourself to play with a
question, and playing means approaching it in every form it comes in: as an
equation, as a picture, as a simulation, as a limiting case, as something you
try to explain to someone else. Only then do you get to trust the answer,
and even then only for now. The things I trust are the things I have taken
apart myself, and I keep a list of the ones I have not.

In practice this shapes how I write exercises. I compose them, in the way a
musician composes a piece, with a theme, a build-up, and a place where the
student has to carry the melody alone. The task is rarely "derive the
result" by itself. It is "derive the result, then implement it, then find
the parameter range where it stops being true." A simulation that produces
the expected figure on the first try is a reason for concern, not
celebration. Finding out why the integration step was too large, or why the
noise term had the wrong scaling, is where the learning happens, and I try
to leave room for that instead of handing out code that already works. A
slider you can move while a model runs does the same job on a smaller
scale, which is why these pages exist.

## Mathematics as a language, not a hurdle

Students arrive in theoretical neuroscience from biology, physics,
psychology, computer science and medicine, and their comfort with
mathematics varies enormously. I do not think the answer is to water the
mathematics down. The answer is to always say what a symbol means in words,
to connect every equation to a picture, and to be explicit about which
steps are routine and which are the actual idea. An eigenvector is a
direction the matrix does not rotate. A Fourier transform asks how much of
each frequency is in a signal. Once that is in place, the algebra is
bookkeeping, and most people can do bookkeeping once they are told that is
all it is. I say this with some authority. My father is a bookkeeper in the
literal sense, a *Steuerberater*, and there was a time when I thought I
would become one too.

In the same spirit, I try never to use an idea from a previous course
without saying so. Being told "you have seen this before" when you have not
is one of the fastest ways to lose someone.

## Confusion is where the good things come from

Behaviour is always multidimensional. The people I teach will confuse me,
and I will confuse them, and I have stopped treating that as a failure of
either side. Some friction is exactly what you want: it is the sign that two
ways of thinking have actually met. The trick is to keep it at a useful
level, enough that something new can come out of it, not so much that
someone gives up. A good deal of teaching, as I now understand it, is
tuning that level.

## Diversity needs support, not just approval

I believe that diverse groups do better science, and the previous section
is part of why. People who think differently ask different questions,
notice different things in the same data, and catch each other's blind
spots. But wanting diversity is not the same as having it. A group that is
open to everyone on paper and then runs on one unspoken set of habits, one
way of speaking up in meetings, one idea of what a productive day looks
like, will quietly lose the people it says it wants. Support has to be
concrete: expectations written down, several ways to contribute and not
just the loudest one, and the willingness to change how the group works
when it is not working for someone.

I say this partly from the inside. I consider myself very neurodiverse.
What I lack in diversity of outer appearance I make up for in inner chaos,
and I have spent a good part of my career working out which structures let
me do my best work and which ones get in the way. That makes me quicker to
notice when a student is struggling with the format rather than the
content, and more willing to change the format.

## Helping each other is the point

Science is not a solo sport, whatever the authorship conventions suggest.
The groups I have enjoyed most, and that produced the best work, were the
ones where asking for help was normal and giving it was expected. I try to
make that the default in anything I run: in exercises, where I would rather
students solve a sheet together and understand it than alone and not; in
the seminar, where feedback on a draft or a practice talk is something
everyone gives and everyone receives; and in supervision, where I want to
be asked early rather than late.

## My time with you

When I supervise someone, our meetings work like office hours. The time I
have reserved is yours, and you can spend it on whatever is most useful to
you right now: the derivation you are stuck on, the figure that will not
come out right, the question of whether a PhD is the right next step, or
something that has nothing to do with the project but is getting in the way
of it. I will tell you at the start how much time I have that day, so that
you can decide what to spend it on. And I will say so when I do not know
the answer.

One small print: I am not a licensed doctor or psychotherapist, so I can
only give oral referrals. They are drawn from vast experience, some of it
my own, and they come with a warm recommendation to also ask someone with
an actual licence.

## Outreach is teaching too

Since 2019 I have helped organise the German Neuroscience Olympiad final in
Frankfurt and run its computational tutorial, and for several years I was
part of the team behind the Night of Science on the Riedberg campus.
Teaching a sixteen-year-old why a neuron is a leaky bucket uses exactly the
same muscles as teaching a master's student about pattern formation, just
with less notation. If anything, the younger audience is less forgiving of
hand-waving, and I have brought more than one explanation back from the
Olympiad into my university teaching because it worked better there.
